name: nbsdgames
why: A collection of NetBSD text games with some old-school charm, though most are familiar classics.

brief.what_it_is: A collection of about two dozen terminal games, written in C with ncurses, that run in a text console. The README lists Jewels, Sudoku, Mines, Reversi, Checkers, Battleship, SOS, Rabbithole, Pipes, Fifteen, Memoblocks, Fisher, Muncher, Miketron, Redsquare, Darrt, Snakeduel, Tugow, Trsr, Scissor and Revenge. Each game is its own executable, and difficulty or board size can be set with command line options. Running the nbsdgames program opens a menu from which the other games can be launched. The input is keystrokes and the output is a curses-drawn board on the terminal.
brief.why_it_exists: The README pitches it as a way to get games onto machines that have no real games left, such as a router, an old 1980s computer, or a spare BSD install, and it is pointed at bored sysadmins and people who need a Reversi AI for homework. It also says plainly that it is not the older bsdgames collection.
brief.how_it_works: The games are plain C programs that draw with ncurses, so they run in any terminal that ncurses supports. Build them from the src directory with make, then install them. The README also says the code has been ported to Windows through PDCurses, to Plan9, and to DOS and SDL platforms. Redsquare is described as Conway's Game of Life made playable, and Trsr is a two-player minesweeper.

commands_seen.cmd: sudo apt install git make gcc libncurses5-dev
commands_seen.context: Installs the build tools and ncurses development headers on Debian-based systems, as given in the README's compile section.
Makes a shallow clone of the repository to get the latest source.
Moves into the source directory where the Makefile lives.
Installs the built binaries system-wide. The README notes you can use the already compiled binaries from your package manager instead.
Run at the terminal to open the fancy menu from which all the games can be started.

brief.install_notes: Packaged for Debian and other DEB distros, OpenSUSE and other RPM distros, AUR, Alpine, FreeBSD, NetBSD, DragonflyBSD, Minix, and Homebrew on macOS. The README warns that distro packages may be old and missing games or fixes, and recommends building from source for the latest version. Building needs git (optional), POSIX make (optional), a C99 compiler, the standard library, and ncurses (libncurses5-dev on Debian). No accounts or runtimes are needed. Scores are saved to disk if the user allows it.
brief.standout: The Darrt and Scissor entries are described as original gameplay rather than clones of classics, and Tugow is a numpad practice game. The project also runs on unusually old or odd platforms: DOS, Plan9, and Windows through PDCurses.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows no release date or last-commit date. It says the project is on many distro repositories and that the author thanks several packagers and contributors, which suggests it is still in use. I did not check the commit history or release list.
brief.caveats: Distro packages can be old and may lack newer games and fixes, so building from source is recommended. Windows support uses PDCurses, OS/2 is untested by the author, and the hardware requirements are written as jokes. Building requires ncurses and a C99 compiler. Only the README was read, so the game list and features are the author's own description.
quotes: Or just enter "nbsdgames" at your terminal to get a fancy menu and play all sorts of games from there.

The difficulty and/or dimensions are adjustable through simple command line options, you can play a minesweeper game that take hours to complete, or exprience hexadecimal sudoku and 8x8 fifteen-like puzzles!
Don't worry anymore as you've got nbsdgames now!
